power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: forms can move us.
A securely fixed sculpture can still look ready to fall and make us uneasy.
Why does this visual pattern affect us when nothing can fall?
We propose that what perceivers evaluate is often not an object as such but structure in sensory signals that carries information about the state and properties of objects and events.
Deformation can indicate stiffness, the relation between mass and support can indicate stability, and visual expansion can signal approach.
When such information matters for what a perceiver does or for what happens to them, the structure that carries it acquires evaluative weight.
This structure is often available before the object is identified, and under poorer conditions: in the periphery, at a distance, in poor light, and for objects never seen before.
Responding to it lets perceivers prepare to act early, at the price of responding wherever the structure appears, including in objects they cannot identify.

Some evaluative influence can remain when the information no longer serves its original use, which we call functional detachment (FD), and it can appear in new objects or events that preserve the same informative structure, which we call structural transfer.
Together, they define functional structural detachment (FSD).
The influence persists in part because a structure with little use in one context remains important in others.

FSD predicts that evaluative influence transfers further when the structure has a broad functional history, having been useful across many different situations, even when perceivers detect it equally well.
We describe experiments that separate this account from salience, processing fluency, simple association, and the valuation of current consequences.

Art provides a limiting case: abstract forms can retain structures that were informative about objects and events elsewhere, and these structures can continue to affect us even when their original source and practical role have become remote.
A sculpture leans beyond its base.
Although it is securely fixed and cannot fall, it can still make a viewer uneasy.
Outside a gallery, the same arrangement would tell us something important: an object may be about to fall.
Why should it still affect us when there is no danger and nothing needs to be done?
The boxes build up the framework one step at a time.
Each ends with a looming example, which applies the definitions of that box to a single case: an object approaching the perceiver.
A perceiver never meets a source directly, whether a vase, a branch or an approaching ball, but only the signal it produces: an image, a video clip or a sound.
The signal X depends on the source S and on external conditions, such as lighting and viewpoint, and it is typically very high-dimensional, with a value for every pixel or every moment.
The source property θ(S) is what matters about the source, both for what happens and for what the perceiver should do.
text.formatted: The source property <ref type="bibr">θ(S)</ref> is what matters about the source, both for what happens and for what the perceiver should do.

text.text: The outcome is what happens to the source, and the payoffs are how good or bad each action is for the perceiver.
Together they make up the source's consequences: the outcome is the part that the perceiver's actions cannot affect, and the payoffs are the part that depends on them.
The source property is fixed by the consequences, never by anyone's evaluations.
For a vase on a shelf, θ is how likely the vase is to tip over and how likely it is to break if it falls.
A structure ϕ(X) and incidental features ψ(X) are features of the signal: maps that reduce a high-dimensional signal to a few numbers.

The structure is source-informative if it tells something about the source property, I (︁ ϕ(X); θ(S) )︁ > 0, where I is mutual information, which is zero exactly when the two variables are independent.
text.formatted: The structure is source-informative if it tells something about the source property, I (︁ ϕ(X); θ(S) )︁ > 0, where I is mutual information, which is zero exactly when the two variables are independent.

text.text: The incidental features add nothing about the source property once the structure is known.

They are needed for two notions central to FSD: structural transfer, in which the learned effect reaches objects whose incidental features were not met before (Box 5), and breadth, the variety of incidental features with which the structure has had consequences (Box 6).
Vase example.
Overhang, the horizontal distance by which the centre of mass lies beyond the edge of its support, is source-informative about tipping.
Colour, texture and decoration are incidental.
Looming example.
For an approaching object, such as a ball, a car, a bird or a cyclist, the source property is the chance that the object is on a collision course, the time to contact and the energy of impact.
The structure is the rate and symmetry of the object's optical expansion: fast, symmetric expansion signals a collision course soon, and lopsided expansion signals that the object will pass by.

Shape, colour and background are incidental provided that all the objects have the same mass and speed; otherwise the kind of object is not incidental, because a car and a ball that expand alike differ in energy of impact.
The link between source-informative structure and evaluation has a biological basis.
The nervous system extracts information about physical properties and events that can guide action.
Human cortical networks are recruited when perceivers predict how physical scenes will unfold, including whether objects will fall or collide (Fischer et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Human cortical networks are recruited when perceivers predict how physical scenes will unfold, including whether objects will fall or collide <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fischer et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Rapid approach provides an even clearer example.

Looming visual structure signals motion towards the perceiver, and human superior colliculus pathways represent both the motion and form of looming objects; these responses are also related to emotional experience (Thieu et al., 2024 (Thieu et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Looming visual structure signals motion towards the perceiver, and human superior colliculus pathways represent both the motion and form of looming objects; these responses are also related to emotional experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Thieu et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Thieu et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Increasing sound intensity likewise carries information about an approaching source and produces greater alertness, bodily arousal (autonomic mobilisation), and emotional responses than receding sound (Bach et al., 2008 (Bach et al., , 2009)).
text.formatted: Increasing sound intensity likewise carries information about an approaching source and produces greater alertness, bodily arousal (autonomic mobilisation), and emotional responses than receding sound <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bach et al., 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bach et al., , 2009))</ref>.

text.text: It is important to note that detecting or orienting to a signal is not the same as evaluating it.
Sudden sensory changes can recruit systems for attentional selection and orienting.

The superior colliculus contributes to target selection and shifts of attention, while cortical networks support both goal-directed and stimulus-driven selection (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Krauzlis et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The superior colliculus contributes to target selection and shifts of attention, while cortical networks support both goal-directed and stimulus-driven selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Corbetta and Shulman, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Krauzlis et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A movement at the edge of the visual field may therefore attract attention and gaze even when, once identified, it has little further significance.
Attention shows that a signal has gained processing priority; it does not by itself show that the signal has acquired positive or negative value.
Perceivers differ, and the same perceiver does not always respond to a signal in the same way.

The task context of an occasion is everything other than the signal that bears on the response: the task the perceiver performs, such as rating or judging, and any information given outside the signal, such as instructions or a label.
For each perceiver r, each signal and each task context, there is a probability distribution of r's responses.
A population Γ is the distribution of perceivers from which participants are drawn.

Both measures below compare two stimuli that show the same objects in the same conditions, with the same incidental features z, and differ only in the structure, which takes the value a in one and b in the other.
In an experiment, the result is checked on a second set of stimuli.
The sensitivity s r (a, b; z) is how well r tells the two stimuli apart in a task about the structure, such as "which overhangs more?".
It is the total variation distance between r's two distributions of responses: 0 when the stimuli cannot be told apart, and 1 when they are never confused.
An ideal observer who sees one response and guesses which stimulus produced it is right with probability 1 2 (1 + s r ).
The evaluative weight is the difference in r's mean rating in an evaluative task, such as rating "how unpleasant is it?"
from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very): where M r (a, z) is r's distribution of ratings of the stimulus with structure a and incidental features z.
Averaging over perceivers r ∼ Γ, and over stimuli whose incidental features are drawn from a distribution Q, gives the population weight
Its sign is the valence: on this scale, a positive weight means that a is rated as more unpleasant than b.
Detecting a structure is not valuing it: the sensitivity can be high while the weight is zero.
Orienting towards a signal is neither; it shows only that the signal has gained processing priority.
Looming example.
Sensitivity is measured by asking "which approaches faster?"
about two video clips of the same object, expanding fast and symmetrically (a) or slowly (b); the weight is how much more unpleasant the fast clip is rated than the slow one.
We call the link between useful source information and its effect on evaluation source-linked valuation.
The effect may be expressed in choice, approach or avoidance, trust, willingness to interact, tension, attraction, aversion, or reported feeling.

This proposal builds on the sensory valuation account of aesthetic experience (Nadal and Skov, 2025), in which valuation involves the transfer of sensory information into neural systems that generate hedonic value and motivational dispositions (to approach or avoid).

text.text: The present framework extends this principle beyond aesthetics to evaluation more broadly.
FSD also adds a more specific question: what happens to evaluative influence linked to informative structure when that structure appears in a different context?
Positive and negative effects fit the same logic.
A pattern that signals reliable support may acquire positive weight, while one that signals instability or collision may acquire negative weight.
What matters is not whether the response is pleasant or unpleasant, but whether evaluation is linked to information carried by the sensory structure.

A structure is consequential if knowing it changes what is likely to happen, or which action is best: seeing that a vase overhangs makes a fall more likely, and makes it worth getting ready to catch the vase.

Formally, the structure either carries information about the outcome, or it has a positive expected value of sample information, the gain in expected payoff from choosing an action after seeing the structure rather than without it.
A history L is a sequence of occasions, each consisting of a source, the conditions, a task and an outcome.
In a consequential history, the outcomes follow the sources, as they do in the world: overhanging vases fall more often.
Its matched history has the same occasions and the same outcomes, but the outcomes are shuffled at random, so that they no longer depend on the sources; this is a yoked-control design.
Q L is the distribution of incidental features of the stimuli seen, which is the same in both histories.
Two groups drawn from one population Γ 0 experience the two histories, giving the populations Γ cons and Γ non .
The consequence effect is the difference between their mean weights (Box 2),
Inherited weight, exposure to the structure and the outcomes themselves are common to both groups and cancel, so W measures the part of the weight learned from the consequences.
Looming example.

The consequential history is a task in virtual reality in which the participant loses points on a collision course unless they dodge; in the matched history, the same collisions are shuffled, so that the expansion no longer predicts them.
The outcome is whether the object is on a collision course, not whether it hits, because whether it hits depends on whether the participant dodges.
The inherited response to looming is common to both groups and cancels in W , so only the learned modulation of looming is tested.
Object recognition can be rapid (Thorpe et al., 1996), but useful sensory information does not always require it.

text.text: Coarse visual structure is available even under brief or peripheral viewing (Schyns and Oliva, 1994; Larson and Loschky, 2009).

text.text: These findings show that sensory information can guide action without full recognition of its kind.
This may help explain why evaluation can depend on informative structure rather than object identity, including when that structure has no immediate practical use (Section 4.1).
Some of this weight is inherited.
Defensive responses to looming are evolutionarily conserved, and in humans looming representations are related to arousal and emotional experience (Thieu et al., 2024).

text.text: Other weights are learned within a lifetime.

The framework connects the two in a simple way: inheritance sets the starting weights, and the perceiver's history of consequences strengthens or weakens them and widens or narrows how far they transfer.
In the boxes, inherited sensitivity belongs to the perceivers' starting point Γ 0 (Box 3), and the definitions compare histories that begin from it.

An inherited weight that no history changes, such as the response to looming, illustrates the link from structure to evaluation, but it is not by itself evidence for detachment; whether it is detached is a question about the history of the species, which the experiments of Section 6 do not address.
Functional detachment (FD) occurs when some evaluative influence remains even though the current situation no longer requires the information to be used in the same way.
Consider physical stability.
The relation between an object's mass and its support carries information about whether it is likely to fall.
People can use visual geometry and material properties to judge stability and predict how objects will behave (Battaglia et al., 2013; Cholewiak et al., 2015; Lupo and Barnett-Cowan, 2015).
text.formatted: People can use visual geometry and material properties to judge stability and predict how objects will behave <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Battaglia et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cholewiak et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lupo and Barnett-Cowan, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: If this information matters-for example, because an object might fall-it can also affect evaluation.
Now change the situation while keeping the stability information visible.
An object is fixed so that it cannot fall.
It no longer has an outcome that depends on its stability.
This is more than reduced actionability: it also removes the outcome itself (Box 4).
Or the visual pattern can be simplified until instability remains visible but the particular object that produced it can no longer be identified.
These changes distinguish reduced actionability, reduced instrumental relevance, and reduced source recoverability.
The latter concerns the identity of the source, not the physical information carried by the signal.
An unfamiliar or abstract structure may still indicate a property and its possible consequences without revealing the object that produced it.
FSD does not require this inference to disappear; Box 4 considers that stronger possibility separately.
Evidence from learning shows that acquired value can outlast what produced it.
In evaluative conditioning, a neutral stimulus, such as an unfamiliar face, is repeatedly shown together with a pleasant or an unpleasant one, and afterwards it is itself liked or disliked more.
This change in liking has been reported to resist extinction: it remains when the stimulus is later shown on its own (Baeyens et al., 1988; Walther et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This change in liking has been reported to resist extinction: it remains when the stimulus is later shown on its own <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baeyens et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Walther et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Learning that one stimulus predicts another behaves differently: fear of a tone that has been followed by a shock fades once the tone is presented without the shock.
Habits also show persistence in action.
A rat trained extensively to press a lever for food keeps pressing after the food has been made unattractive, for example by pairing it with mild illness (Dickinson, 1985).
text.formatted: A rat trained extensively to press a lever for food keeps pressing after the food has been made unattractive, for example by pairing it with mild illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dickinson, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, a rat with limited training does not develop a habit and presses less often.
The extensively trained response is set off by the situation rather than by the current value of the food.

Both evaluative conditioning and habits exhibit functional detachment: a liking or a response acquired through a link to something of value persists after the link has been broken or the value removed.
Neither finding, however, shows which part of the signal this liking or response attaches to.
FSD proposes that it is the source-informative structure.
A change of situation keeps the source property as it was defined in the reference situation, but reduces how much the perceiver depends on the source.

It can do so in five ways: (a) Actionability: the payoff of each action no longer depends on the source property, as when the vase is behind glass: whether or not the vase would tip, getting ready to catch it brings the same payoff.
(b) Instrumental relevance: the payoffs still depend on the source property, but one action is best whatever its value, so the structure no longer helps the perceiver choose.

(c) Kind recoverability: the signal is transformed, for example redrawn as an outline, so that the kind of object can no longer be identified, while the property, such as whether the object would tip, still can.
(d) Property recoverability: the signal is transformed so that the property can no longer be inferred, although the structure is still seen.
(e) Representation: the source is a picture or a sculpture, which shows the structure but has no consequences: a painting of a vase cannot fall.
Types (a) and (b) change the payoffs, (c) and (d) the signals, and (e) the sources.
Type (d) tests a stronger claim, that value attaches to the structure even when the property cannot be inferred; FSD does not require it.
After the change, the two groups of Box 3 are tested again.
Quantities measured after the change carry the subscript rsd, for reduced source dependence.

For a distribution Q of incidental features, the consequence effect after the change, W rsd (Q), is defined as W (Q) in Box 3, but measured after the change: in the evaluative task context of the new situation for (a), (b) and (e), and with the transformed stimuli for (c) and (d).
Q rsd is the distribution of incidental features shown after the change: those of the history for (a)-(d), and those of the representations for (e).
Functional detachment holds if
It is valence-preserving if, in addition, W rsd (Q rsd )/W (Q L ) ≥ δ for a stated fraction δ between 0 and 1: the learned effect keeps its sign and at least that fraction of its size.
Because W rsd compares the two groups, effects of novelty, fluency or the change itself act on both and cancel.

Looming example. (a) The participant watches seated in a cinema, where dodging achieves nothing. (b) In the virtual-reality task, a shield blocks every collision, so that staying put is always the best action. (c) The video clips are redrawn as abstract discs with the same expansion; participants cannot say what the object is, but can still judge whether it would hit them. (d) This type is hard to realise for looming, because expansion is read almost automatically as approach; an expanding ring without depth cues might work.
Looming is therefore a good case for FSD but a weak one for the stronger claim. (e) Films of approaching objects, such as the Lumière brothers' train; a film never collides with its viewer.
Functional detachment means that, in the cinema, the consequential group still finds fast expansion more unpleasant than the matched group does, by at least ∆.
The term functional detachment has previously been used in interbehavioural psychology in a different sense (Ribes and López, 1985).

text.text: Here it refers specifically to this persistence of evaluative influence after reduced dependence on the original source or use.
FD alone is not enough for FSD.
An effect could persist while remaining tied to one particular object.
The next step is therefore to ask whether evaluative influence follows the informative structure into new objects or events.
Stability relations can be preserved across objects that differ in appearance (Battaglia et al., 2013; Cholewiak et al., 2015; Lupo and Barnett-Cowan, 2015).
text.formatted: Stability relations can be preserved across objects that differ in appearance <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Battaglia et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cholewiak et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lupo and Barnett-Cowan, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Structural transfer predicts that evaluative influence tracks the preserved mass-support relation, while visually similar objects with different stability relations should not show the same transfer.
Not all of these objects have the same consequences, and not all of them are single objects.
A single rigid object, such as a vase, stays up as long as its centre of mass lies over its support, and for an ordinary vase its overhang is a good guide to where that is.
A stack of books is several objects, and it stays up only if, at every level, the books above have their combined centre of mass over the book beneath.

A well-built stack can therefore extend surprisingly far: with books of unit length, one to a level, the top book can project by half the harmonic sum 1 + 1 2 + 1 3 + • • • + 1 n , which grows without bound as books are added, a result known since nineteenth-century textbooks of mechanics (Phear, 1850; see Paterson and Zwick, 2009).
text.formatted: A well-built stack can therefore extend surprisingly far: with books of unit length, one to a level, the top book can project by half the harmonic sum 1 + 1 2 + 1 3 + • • • + 1 n , which grows without bound as books are added, a result known since nineteenth-century textbooks of mechanics (Phear, 1850; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Paterson and Zwick, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: A rigid object of the same shape would also stay up, but the converse fails: the top of a stack can slide off even when a rigid object of the same shape would stand, because the stack must satisfy a condition at every level, not only one for the whole.
What the overhang says about tipping, and what counts as a single source, therefore depend on the object.
A clean test of the role of consequences therefore needs a single rigid object, such as a wooden vase of the same shape as a porcelain one.
It tips exactly as the porcelain vase does, so its overhang carries the same information about tipping, but it does not shatter, and its material shows that it will not.
A perceiver who values objects by their current consequences should give the overhanging wooden vase much less weight than the porcelain one.
If value has become attached to the information that the mass-support structure carries about tipping, the wooden vase should carry much of the weight learned on porcelain.
A weight for the wooden vase close to that for the porcelain vase therefore separates FSD from the valuation of current consequences (Section 6.3).

The stack of books answers a different question: whether perceivers, who often judge stability well (Battaglia et al., 2013), track the support relations of a composite object rather than its overall overhang.
text.formatted: The stack of books answers a different question: whether perceivers, who often judge stability well <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Battaglia et al., 2013)</ref>, track the support relations of a composite object rather than its overall overhang.

text.text: Research on analogy and relational learning shows that perceivers can recognise common structure across examples that differ in their surface properties (Gentner and Markman, 1997; Kurtz et al., 2013).

text.text: Learned fear, too, generalises along conceptual categories and not only along perceptual similarity (Dunsmoor and Murphy, 2015): what transfers depends on how the learned stimulus is represented.
text.formatted: Learned fear, too, generalises along conceptual categories and not only along perceptual similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dunsmoor and Murphy, 2015)</ref>: what transfers depends on how the learned stimulus is represented.

text.text: FSD builds on this capacity in a specific way: evaluative influence acquired through useful source information should follow the preserved structure into new stimuli.

Structural transfer asks whether the learned effect follows the structure into new objects: objects with the same structure but with incidental features never met in the history, such as lamps and sculptures after a history with vases.
Q novel is the distribution of these new incidental features; none of them occurred in the history.
Provided that source-linked valuation holds, |W (Q L )| ≥ ∆, the transfer index compares the learned effect on the new objects with that on the objects of the history, in the same task:
T = 1 is full transfer, T = 0 is none, and values in between are partial transfer.
Structural transfer holds if T ≈ 1, that is, T lies within a tolerance of 1 that is fixed before the data are collected.

Transfer should come from what was learned, not from reasoning: a participant who has noticed that, say, tall objects with a narrow base tend to fall, and applies this as a rule to the new objects, is not showing structural transfer, so participants are asked afterwards how they made their ratings.
In statistical terms, transfer is the absence of an interaction between the structure and the incidental features in the learned effect.
The new objects must have the same consequences as the old ones, such as being equally fragile; objects that tip but do not break, such as stacks of books, are a separate test (Section 4.2).
Functional structural detachment (FSD) holds when functional detachment and structural transfer occur together, after the same change of situation (Box 4) and for the same new objects:
Looming example.
The new objects are drones after a history with balls, with the same mass and speed.
FSD means that, in the cinema and with drones, the learned effect both survives and transfers.
5 Functional history

Functional history is the range of situations in which the same informative structure has proved useful, within a perceiver's lifetime or across cultural practices that preserve structures beyond their original settings (Donald, 1991).
text.formatted: Functional history is the range of situations in which the same informative structure has proved useful, within a perceiver's lifetime or across cultural practices that preserve structures beyond their original settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Donald, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Perception can preserve such source information despite substantial changes in the sensory signal.
Human observers, for example, can judge physical properties of soft materials across different shapes and motions, suggesting representations that go beyond raw image similarity (Bi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Human observers, for example, can judge physical properties of soft materials across different shapes and motions, suggesting representations that go beyond raw image similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Neural systems involved in intuitive physics likewise respond when perceivers predict how physical scenes will unfold (Fischer et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Neural systems involved in intuitive physics likewise respond when perceivers predict how physical scenes will unfold <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fischer et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This capacity is important for FSD because the same informative structure must be recognised despite changes in the object that carries it.
Experience can also change how sensory information is represented and used.
Perceptual learning produces lasting changes across sensory and higher cortical systems, and some of these changes can transfer beyond the conditions in which they were acquired (Li, 2016).
text.formatted: Perceptual learning produces lasting changes across sensory and higher cortical systems, and some of these changes can transfer beyond the conditions in which they were acquired <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Li, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: FSD predicts different roles for consequence and breadth: consequential experience should affect how much evaluative weight a structure carries, whereas the breadth of that experience should determine how far its evaluative influence transfers across objects and contexts, beyond recognition or familiarity alone.
The interaction between breadth and consequence is the framework's sharpest prediction.
Exposure and fluency predict that breadth extends transfer whether or not the structure had consequences; FSD predicts that breadth matters more after consequential histories.
The senses add a further dimension of breadth.
Some structures can reach the perceiver through more than one sense: the periodic weave of a tweed jacket can be seen and felt, and a rhythm can be heard, seen and felt.
Such structures are often called amodal, because the same information is carried whatever the sense (Bahrick and Lickliter, 2000).
text.formatted: Such structures are often called amodal, because the same information is carried whatever the sense <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bahrick and Lickliter, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: If the sense through which a structure arrives is treated as one of its incidental features, a structure met in several senses has a broader functional history than one met in only one, and its evaluative influence should transfer further.
Transfer between senses would be the strongest form of structural transfer, because the structure must then be represented independently of any one sense.
There is evidence that such structure is shared across senses.

Touch and hearing appear to share channels for temporal frequency: sounds change the perceived frequency of vibrations on the skin, and vibrations change the perceived frequency of sounds (Yau et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Touch and hearing appear to share channels for temporal frequency: sounds change the perceived frequency of vibrations on the skin, and vibrations change the perceived frequency of sounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Yau et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Five-month-old infants learn a new rhythm when it is presented to sight and hearing together, but not to either alone (Bahrick and Lickliter, 2000), and adults match features across senses systematically, such as pitch with size and with brightness (Spence, 2011).
text.formatted: Five-month-old infants learn a new rhythm when it is presented to sight and hearing together, but not to either alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bahrick and Lickliter, 2000)</ref>, and adults match features across senses systematically, such as pitch with size and with brightness <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Spence, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Two cautions apply: recognising the same structure in two senses, as when the weave of a cloth recalls a rhythm in music, is not yet evaluation.

FSD requires that value acquired through one sense appears in another, and that the structure has mattered somewhere, as the periodicity of a texture does for grip and handling, or that of footsteps for approach.
In addition, periodicity in music can be valued through expectation (Section 7.1), which lies outside the present framework.
The breadth of a consequential history is the variety of incidental features with which the structure has had consequences.
It is computed only from the occasions on which something consequential happened, such as a collision with an approaching object.
Breadth is the conditional entropy, in bits, of the incidental features given the structure on those occasions:
It is zero when every value of the structure always came with the same incidental features, and it grows as the structure has mattered in more varied objects.

To compute it, take each value of the structure in turn, find the probability of each kind of object among the occasions with that value, compute the entropy of these probabilities, and average the entropies over the values.
For example, suppose the approaching objects expand either fast or slowly, each on half of the collisions.
In a narrow history every collision is with a ball; in a broad history the collisions are equally often with four kinds of object, a ball, a box, a bird and a car.

The framework predicts that a broader history transfers further.

A broad and a narrow consequential history, each with its matched control, are given to groups drawn from the same population, and their transfer indices (Box 5) are compared for the same new objects:
The groups must be equally sensitive to the structure (Box 2), so that breadth affects valuation and not merely how well the structure is perceived.
Because each transfer index is computed from consequence effects, any effect of breadth that also appears in the matched groups, as mere exposure or fluency would produce, cancels.
A narrow history contains collisions with balls only; a broad one contains collisions with many kinds of object, all of the same mass and speed.
The prediction is that, for drones, the broad history gives the larger transfer index, provided that the groups are equally good at telling the two rates of expansion apart.
The argument of Section 3 adds a second prediction.

If evaluative weight attaches to structure because structure is available early, detachment and transfer should be strongest for coarse structure that is available at brief exposures and in the periphery, such as an overall masssupport relation or optical expansion, and weaker for fine detail that becomes available only once the object has been identified.
How could the nervous system preserve the link between an informative structure and its evaluative significance while objects and contexts change?
No single neural mechanism is required by FSD.
Several established systems could provide different parts of the process.
The first requirement is a representation of the relevant source property.

Research on intuitive physics, material perception, and auditory event perception shows that sensory systems extract information about physical causes rather than responding only to local features of the signal (properties of small regions of it, such as the brightness, colour, or orientation of an edge at one location) (Fischer et al., 2016; Fleming, 2017; Winkler and Denham, 2024; Bi et al., 2025).

Experience can modify these links.

text.text: A model-based value is computed when it is needed, from a model of the consequences, so it disappears as soon as the consequences do, for example when the vase is fixed down (the valuation of current consequences, a rival to FSD; Section 6.1).

A model-free, or cached, value is stored with a state and changed only by new experience, so it persists after the reward has lost its value (functional detachment; Box 4), as habits do (Section 4.1).

What a cached value carries over to depends on the state it is stored with: if that state is the informative structure rather than the particular object, the value follows the structure to new objects (structural transfer; Box 5).
Learned value generalises to stimuli according to their similarity to the rewarded one, and the breadth of this generalisation relates to hippocampal-striatal connectivity (Kahnt et al., 2012).

text.text: On this proposal, a simulation-based model supplies the source property, and a model-free learner attaches value to the structure.
FSD also predicts a specific pattern of neural activity.

Representations should distinguish graded values of the relevant source property across different objects within the appropriate physical class, rather than merely resemble one another across all objects.
These representations should be linked to appetitive or aversive responses in valuation-related brain systems, depending on the consequences signalled by the structure.

This link should remain detectable when the structure appears in new objects or contexts without immediate practical use, and broader consequential functional history should increase its range of transfer.
These mechanisms make FSD biologically plausible, but its central predictions require behavioural tests of functional detachment and structural transfer (Section 6).
The same informative structure need not carry the same evaluative weight for every perceiver.
Experience can change what is detected, which aspects of a signal are treated as informative, and how strongly those aspects influence evaluation.
Perceptual learning can increase sensitivity to information that has repeatedly proved useful, while broader experience can shape how source properties are represented and used.
These differences can extend beyond perception itself.
One perceiver may simply experience an object as unstable, while another may explicitly recognise the mass-support configuration that produces that impression.
Cultural experience can add another layer.
The same musical or visual structure may be evaluated differently across perceivers whose preferences have developed in different cultural environments.
Music preferences, for example, vary systematically across social and geographic contexts (Mellander et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Music preferences, for example, vary systematically across social and geographic contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Mellander et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Perceiver history therefore both produces and modulates FSD: it shapes which informative structures are detected (Box 2), how much evaluative weight they carry (Box 3), and how far their influence transfers (Boxes 5 and 6).
6 Rival accounts and tests 6.1 Related and rival accounts FSD builds on several established accounts that explain different parts of the proposed sequence.
Some provide a mechanism or principle that FSD brings together with the others; others are rivals, which explain some of the same effects without source-linked valuation.
The tests of Section 6.3 separate FSD from the rivals.

The sensory valuation account provides a particularly close foundation for FSD. Nadal and Skov (2025) propose that sensory information is transferred to valuation systems, where it contributes to positive or negative hedonic value and motivational dispositions.
text.formatted: The sensory valuation account provides a particularly close foundation for FSD. <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Nadal and Skov (2025)</ref> propose that sensory information is transferred to valuation systems, where it contributes to positive or negative hedonic value and motivational dispositions.

text.text: They also emphasise that valuation is shaped by learned experience and current behavioural conditions.
This directly supports the link between sensory information and evaluative weight assumed by FSD.
FSD extends this account by explaining how the functional significance of sensory information may determine which features of sensory structure acquire evaluative weight.
It further asks whether this influence persists when the structure's immediate practical role changes and transfers with that structure to new objects and contexts.
Intuitive physical inference explains how perceivers use sensory structure to predict an object's behaviour.
For example, the relation between mass and support helps them judge whether an object will fall (Battaglia et al., 2013; Cholewiak et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For example, the relation between mass and support helps them judge whether an object will fall <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Battaglia et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cholewiak et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Such predictions can influence evaluation.
FSD adds that the same stability pattern can affect evaluation even when an object cannot fall, and that this effect can appear in other objects with the same pattern.
Predictive-processing accounts explain how the brain uses past experience to predict sensory information and update its expectations.
Prediction and prediction error can also influence perception and aesthetic experience (Van de Cruys and Wagemans, 2011; Van de Cruys et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Prediction and prediction error can also influence perception and aesthetic experience (Van de Cruys and Wagemans, 2011; <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Van de Cruys et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This provides an important basis for FSD: experience can shape how informative structure is perceived and evaluated.
FSD makes a more specific prediction about what carries this influence across contexts.

Evaluative weight acquired through useful source information should remain linked to the informative structure when its immediate role changes and should follow that structure into new objects or events.
Salience and learned attention.
Sudden or behaviourally relevant structure attracts attention (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002), and a cue that predicts an outcome gains attention and is learned about faster (Mackintosh, 1975).
text.formatted: Sudden or behaviourally relevant structure attracts attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Corbetta and Shulman, 2002)</ref>, and a cue that predicts an outcome gains attention and is learned about faster <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Mackintosh, 1975</ref>).

text.text: An overhanging object that has fallen before may therefore be looked at more.
Attention, however, has no sign: it predicts that a structure is processed more, not that it is liked or disliked.
Processing fluency explains why stimuli that are easier to process are often evaluated more positively (Reber et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Processing fluency explains why stimuli that are easier to process are often evaluated more positively <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Reber et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: FSD suggests that fluency may also result from functional history.
Repeated use of the same informative structure across different objects and situations may strengthen its neural representation and make it easier to process.
Research on perceptual learning shows that behavioural relevance and experience can shape neural plasticity (Roelfsema et al., 2010; Li, 2016).
text.formatted: Research on perceptual learning shows that behavioural relevance and experience can shape neural plasticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Roelfsema et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Li, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Synaptic strengthening, including long-term potentiation, is one possible mechanism (Cooke and Bear, 2014).
text.formatted: Synaptic strengthening, including long-term potentiation, is one possible mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cooke and Bear, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Fluency may therefore be partly a consequence of the same functional history that gives a structure evaluative weight.
However, processing ease alone does not explain why that structure carries positive or negative significance.
Structural and relational learning explains how perceivers recognise the same pattern in objects that look different (Gentner and Markman, 1997; Kurtz et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Structural and relational learning explains how perceivers recognise the same pattern in objects that look different <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gentner and Markman, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kurtz et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: But recognition alone does not explain why the pattern affects evaluation.
FSD links this influence to the useful information the pattern carries about its source.
The influence can also appear in new objects, even when that information has no immediate practical use.
A perceiver may value an object by working out, here and now, what it will do, as in model-based reinforcement learning (Daw et al., 2005).
text.formatted: A perceiver may value an object by working out, here and now, what it will do, as in model-based reinforcement learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Daw et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Such a value disappears as soon as the consequences do, and it requires the object and its situation to be represented.
It predicts no functional detachment.
Is this just conditioning?
At the level of the learning rule, it may well be: a structure is paired with consequences and acquires value.

What FSD adds is a claim about the unit of learning, the source-informative structure rather than the object or its appearance; a reason why that unit is privileged, namely that it carries information about consequential properties and is available early (Section 3); and a prediction of where the value goes, to new objects that preserve the structure, as far as the functional history extends.

The distinctive prediction is that evaluative influence remains linked to source-informative structure across changes in practical use and object identity, with the scope of transfer shaped by functional history.
The following seven steps set out the logic of a test, from independently established physical information to evaluative transfer and functional history.
Studies of existing responses and controlled learning histories answer different questions (Section 6.4).

Start with a structure whose physical significance can be verified independently, such as looming or mass-support relations (Fischer et al., 2016; Schwettmann et al., 2019; Thieu et al., 2024 Thieu et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Start with a structure whose physical significance can be verified independently, such as looming or mass-support relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fischer et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Schwettmann et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Thieu et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Thieu et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Different properties should be tested separately.
Verify that the structure predicts a physical property or event independently of evaluation and that perceivers use it to guide an appropriate action; attracting attention alone is not enough.

Test whether neural activity distinguishes graded values of that property across different objects within the appropriate physical class, rather than tracking appearance or object identity alone (Section 6.4).
Measure whether variation in the source property contributes to positive or negative behavioural evaluation, separately from attention and arousal.
Neural activity in valuation-related systems can corroborate this link, but source-linked valuation alone does not establish FSD.
Determine whether evaluative influence remains when the same informative structure loses its immediate practical role, as in a securely fixed object (Box 4).
The source property may remain perceptible; FD does not require loss of property inference.
Present unfamiliar objects that preserve the informative relation but change incidental features, alongside controls that resemble the original objects while changing that relation (Box 5).
The decisive behavioural test combines Steps 5 and 6: persistence and transfer must occur together in new objects under changed practical circumstances.
Compare the reach of transfer after broad and narrow consequential histories, distinguishing functional breadth from exposure or improved structure discrimination (Box 6).
Controlled learning histories are needed to test whether experience causes this difference.
Convergent evidence would connect independently verified source information, neural representation of the relevant property, behavioural evaluation, and the joint FD-transfer effect.
Neural evidence can support this account without proving a specific causal mechanism.
Table 1 compares FSD with rival predictions across ten tests.
Some can examine existing responses, while tests involving consequential and matched histories or learned cue contingencies require controlled experience to isolate causal effects.
The structure provides information about its source property, whatever the particular object or signal.
Salience: a conspicuous signal attracts attention but need not indicate a source property.
Judgements track independently verified source properties rather than perceptual prominence alone.
This establishes a prerequisite, not FSD itself.
A consequential history and a matched, yoked history with the same objects and the same number of falls, assigned to trials independently of stability, so that salience and familiarity are matched.
Informative structure influences evaluation according to the consequences it indicates, which may be positive or negative.
Salience or fluency: evaluation reflects attention or ease of processing, which are the same in both histories, so no difference is predicted.
A larger evaluative weight after the consequential history than after the yoked one.
Present the structure in a fixed object or harmless representation; consider the wooden-vase diagnostic separately (Section 4.2).
Some learned evaluative influence persists when its immediate practical role is removed.
Valuation of current consequences: evaluation depends on present outcomes and should decline when the object is fixed.
A structure-specific evaluative effect persists when the property remains perceptible but its former practical consequences are absent.
Structural transfer.
Present unfamiliar objects or signals that preserve the informative relation while changing appearance, material, or modality, and objects that resemble the trained ones but differ in the relation.
Evaluative influence follows the preserved informative relation into new objects or contexts.
Surface-based association or fluency: evaluation generalises according to perceptual similarity or familiarity.
Evaluation follows the informative relation despite changes in irrelevant surface features, rather than following surface resemblance.
Sign of valuation.
The same informative relation has negative consequences in one group (an unprepared fall costs points) and positive consequences in another (a prepared fall earns points).
The direction of evaluative influence depends on the consequences associated with the information, not on its salience.
Salience, learned attention, or fluency: greater processing priority or ease does not by itself predict the sign of evaluation.
The direction of evaluation changes with consequential experience while the informative relation is preserved.

Breadth of functional history.
Four histories, narrow or broad and consequential or not, with matched exposure and equal sensitivity to the structure.
Broader consequential experience increases the range of objects and contexts to which evaluative influence transfers.
General exposure, perceptual learning, or fluency: broader experience may improve recognition or fluency, but equally with and without consequences.
Elemental association predicts the same interaction, so this test does not exclude it.
Breadth increases evaluative transfer specifically when the structure has been consequential, beyond differences in recognition, exposure, and fluency.
Neural representation and valuation.
Measure representations of source-informative structure and valuation-related responses across different objects and contexts.
Neural activity distinguishes values of the source property across object classes, and its relation with positive or negative valuation persists after the immediate practical role changes.
Physical representation without detached valuation: neural coding of a source property generalises, but evaluative responses depend on current consequences or reward.
Cross-object representations of the property remain associated with evaluative responses in new contexts without immediate practical consequences.
Conflict between cues.
During learning, an incidental feature such as colour predicts falls as well as the structure does; the two are separated at test.
The structure acquires more evaluative weight, and transfers further, than the equally predictive incidental feature.
Simple association: both cues acquire value according to their predictive history alone.
More weight and more transfer for the structure than for the incidental feature.
Present brief stimuli, measure source identification and independently verify that the informative structure is discriminable.
FSD permits evaluative weight without source identification but does not require identification to fail.
no weight is expected when source identity cannot be recovered.
Weight despite chance-level identification would support an identificationindependent route; its absence would not by itself refute FSD.

A structure, such as the periodicity of a texture, is met in two senses (seen and felt) or in one (seen), with or without consequences and with equal sensitivity; evaluation is tested in a third sense (heard).
Two-sense histories increase transfer to the third sense more after consequential histories.
Fluency, or learning confined to one sense: no greater cross-sense transfer after consequential two-sense histories.
Transfer to the third sense is greater after consequential two-sense histories, beyond differences in sensitivity.

The decisive behavioural test combines functional detachment and structural transfer; the remaining comparisons establish prerequisites, distinguish rival explanations, or test the proposed mechanisms.
Boxes 1-6 specify the formal comparisons; the following points concern their operationalisation.
Source information and behaviour.
Establish the relevant source property, informative structure, and action relevance independently of evaluation, as in Steps 1-2 (Boxes 1 and 2).
Perceptual sensitivity and evaluation.
Measure structure discrimination separately from positive or negative evaluation, attention, and arousal under comparable stimulus conditions (Box 2).
Cross-object decoding should distinguish graded values of the relevant source property within an appropriate physical class, with distinct training and test object families.

Relate those representations to independently measured behavioural evaluation and valuation-related activity (including amygdala, insula, orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and striatum), controlling for appearance, attention, arousal, and expected consequences.
Correlation alone cannot establish neural causation.
Test the changes listed in Box 4 (Step 5), without requiring source-property inference to disappear.
Loss of source identity and loss of information about the property are distinct tests.
Structural transfer.
New objects must preserve the informative relation while differing in incidental features (Box 5).
Other stimuli should preserve surface similarity while changing the informative relation.

The relevant physical consequences should be comparable when testing structural transfer itself; fragile objects provide a cleaner comparison than sources with substantially different consequences of falling.
Detachment and transfer should be tested after the same change of situation.
An evaluative effect that persists for familiar objects, combined with an unrelated effect in new objects, would not establish their joint occurrence.
Functional history.
Existing responses may reflect extensive learning, inherited dispositions, or both.
Studies without experimental learning can identify stable sensory-evaluative relationships and their transfer, but cannot isolate how those relationships developed.
The formal definition of source-linked valuation in Box 3 requires a comparison between consequential and matched non-consequential histories.
This can be approximated through controlled experience with a structure whose physical meaning is already established.
Participants in the consequential condition encounter outcomes that depend on the relevant property.
Matched participants encounter the same stimuli and overall distribution of outcomes, but without that dependence.
To test breadth, these conditions are combined with broad and narrow experience across object families (Box 6).
Perceptual sensitivity should be comparable before evaluating transfer.
Longer-term or repeated experience may be preferable when the aim is to examine enduring changes in evaluative influence.
Brief training can test learning effects, but should not be assumed to recreate neural mechanisms established through extensive experience or evolution.
Formal criteria.
The boxes define the learned evaluative contribution as the difference between consequential and matched histories.
FD requires that this difference remain meaningfully different from zero after reduced source dependence (Box 4).
Structural transfer requires that the learned effect extend to novel incidental features according to the transfer criterion (Box 5).
FSD requires both effects under the same change and for the same new features (Box 5).
These criteria distinguish the formal causal claim from observations of existing responses.

A stable behavioural and neural relationship across objects and contexts strongly supports the proposed mechanism, but does not by itself establish the difference between consequential and non-consequential histories required by the current formal definitions.
Quantitative predictions.
Evaluative transfer can be measured across increasing differences in the incidental features of objects.
These differences should be defined independently of evaluation.
The resulting transfer gradient can then be related to functional history.
The prediction is that broader consequential experience increases the range of transfer beyond any improvement in recognising the structure.
A graded transfer model can describe this relationship without assuming that the underlying neuronal representations are fixed or identical across stimuli.
Looming offers a bridge from biologically significant structure (Section 3) to artistic representation: optical expansion signals approach even when no collision with the perceiver is possible.
The information itself does not determine one fixed response.
A ball approaching during play may invite interception, whereas a vehicle approaching while crossing a road calls for avoidance.
The same kind of source information can therefore contribute differently to evaluation depending on the current context.
Now move the structure further from its ordinary source.
A film can reproduce optical expansion or approaching sound even though nothing is physically moving towards the viewer.
The best-known early case is visual: the Lumière brothers' Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat.

The popular story that its first audiences fled in panic is not supported by contemporary sources (Bottomore, 1999; Loiperdinger, 2004), but early viewers did describe being startled by the approaching locomotive while knowing that it was only an image. Gorky (1896 Gorky ( /1972) ) wrote that the train seemed about to rush into the darkened hall, and at once reminded himself that it was only a shadow; Gunning (1989 Gunning ( /1994) ) accordingly locates the film's effect in the conflict between what spectators knew and what they saw.

text.text: The cinema also bears out the earlier argument that the strength of such an effect depends on the observer and on their learning history.
Audiences who have seen countless approaching objects on screen appear to react less strongly to such shots today.

There are no measurements that allow a direct historical comparison, and early reactions also reflected the novelty of moving images as such (Gunning, 1989 (Gunning, /1994), but experimental work shows how such attenuation can arise without abolishing the underlying response.

text.text: More generally, extinction does not erase the original learning but adds context-dependent inhibitory learning (Bouton, 2004).
text.formatted: More generally, extinction does not erase the original learning but adds context-dependent inhibitory learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bouton, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Observers also differ: the perceived time-to-collision of approaching objects depends on their threat value, and the size of this bias scales with self-reported fear (Vagnoni et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Observers also differ: the perceived time-to-collision of approaching objects depends on their threat value, and the size of this bias scales with self-reported fear <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Vagnoni et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The response to approach structure is thus not a fixed reflex but a valuation that differs between observers and is updated by experience.

This is the kind of extension predicted by FSD: evaluative influence can remain attached to informative structure when its immediate practical role changes; in the cinema, learning attenuates this influence without removing it, so that it remains available wherever approach still has consequences.
Other representations can likewise preserve deformation or precarious mass-support structure without reproducing their normal sources or outcomes (Section 4.1).
Abstract art can extend this separation without requiring identification of a depicted object.
We call the contribution of such preserved evaluative influence to aesthetic experience aesthetic recruitment.
An artwork recruits a structure whose functional significance was established in other contexts and uses its evaluative influence as one component of the perceiver's response.

This proposal fits a broader neurobiological view in which aesthetic experience arises through the valuation of sensory information rather than through a mechanism unique to art (Nadal and Skov, 2025).
text.formatted: This proposal fits a broader neurobiological view in which aesthetic experience arises through the valuation of sensory information rather than through a mechanism unique to art <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Nadal and Skov, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: FSD adds a functional-history claim: some of the evaluative influence recruited in art may have been acquired because the preserved structure carried useful information in other contexts.
In ordinary perception, the object that produces the signal is the object whose property matters.

In art the two come apart: the implied source, such as the vase that would tip, may be depicted, suggested or absent, while a representation, such as a painting, a sculpture or a film, produces the signal.
A representation has no consequences of its own: a painting of a vase cannot fall.
The structure was therefore informative where it was learned, but says nothing about the representation:
The artist can set the structure freely, including to combinations that no physical object could produce.

A structure is a candidate aesthetic primitive if three conditions hold: (i) it was source-informative in the history (Box 1); (ii) perceivers detect it in representations (Box 2); (iii) functional structural detachment holds when the sources are replaced by representations, type (e) of Box 4 (Box 5).
The film is the representation and the depicted train is the implied source.
Optical expansion is a candidate aesthetic primitive if participants detect it in films and FSD holds for films.
This agrees with Thieu et al. (2024), who describe visual looming as a primitive for human emotion.
text.formatted: This agrees with <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Thieu et al. (2024)</ref>, who describe visual looming as a primitive for human emotion.

text.text: The evaluative influence that a work recruits in this way, such as the tension contributed by a precarious configuration, does not determine the evaluation of the whole work.

FSD explains why tension or unease can arise in front of a work without a mechanism specific to art: negative and positive weights are two poles of the same evaluative dimension, so no separate mechanism is needed to produce a negative response.
FSD does not by itself explain why a work that evokes tension or unease is valued and sought, which is the real puzzle of negative emotion in art.
That puzzle arises only if the evaluation of a work equals the valence of its components.

Aesthetic experience combines perceptual processing with emotion and valuation, meaning, knowledge and context (Chatterjee and Vartanian, 2014), and negative affect can contribute to positive engagement with art (Menninghaus et al., 2017; Schindler et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Aesthetic experience combines perceptual processing with emotion and valuation, meaning, knowledge and context <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chatterjee and Vartanian, 2014)</ref>, and negative affect can contribute to positive engagement with art <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Menninghaus et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Schindler et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: If evaluation has several components, a negative one is one input among others.
We claim only that FSD supplies some of these components, not how they are combined.
Perceiver history remains important here.
Experience can affect which structures are detected, how strongly they influence evaluation, and how they are interpreted.
In visual art, previously formed concept networks may help perceivers interpret abstract structure and con-nect it with existing knowledge (Rogala et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In visual art, previously formed concept networks may help perceivers interpret abstract structure and con-nect it with existing knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Rogala et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Artists can exploit these differences by preserving, amplifying, or transforming informative structure in new contexts.

The empirical task is therefore to establish the functional history of the structure first and then test whether its evaluative influence continues to follow that structure into artistic representations.
Music is a particularly clear case of FSD, and it separates two routes to value that visual art tends to combine.
A song keeps an implied source: a singer whose voice carries information about arousal, effort and emotional state, much as figurative art keeps a depicted object.
Lyrics add meaning by linguistic convention, which lies outside the structures considered here.
Instrumental music keeps the structure while removing the source, as abstract art does (Box 4, type (e)).
Several of its structures are inherited from consequential sources.
Emotion is expressed in music performance with the same acoustic cues as in vocal expression, among them tempo, loudness, pitch level and contour, and timbre (Juslin and Laukka, 2003).
text.formatted: Emotion is expressed in music performance with the same acoustic cues as in vocal expression, among them tempo, loudness, pitch level and contour, and timbre <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Juslin and Laukka, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The final slowing of performed pieces follows the deceleration of runners coming to a stop (Friberg and Sundberg, 1999).
text.formatted: The final slowing of performed pieces follows the deceleration of runners coming to a stop <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Friberg and Sundberg, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: A crescendo has the structure of rising sound intensity, a warning cue for an approaching source (Bach et al., 2009).
text.formatted: A crescendo has the structure of rising sound intensity, a warning cue for an approaching source <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bach et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: In each case the structure was informative about a voice, a moving body or an approaching object, and instrumental music presents it with no such source: a candidate for functional detachment and structural transfer.
Reward and prediction.
Music engages the reward system.

Intensely pleasurable passages activate brain regions implicated in reward (Blood and Zatorre, 2001); dopamine is released in the caudate while a peak is anticipated and in the nucleus accumbens when it arrives (Salimpoor et al., 2011); and interactions between the nucleus accumbens and auditory cortex predict how much listeners will pay for unfamiliar music (Salimpoor et al., 2013).

text.text: Much of this reward tracks prediction.

Listeners learn the statistics of their musical system and form expectations about what comes next (Huron, 2006; Pearce, 2018), and pleasure in chord sequences depends jointly on the uncertainty of the context and the surprise of the event (Cheung et al., 2019).

text.text: Tonal syntax predicts the continuation of the music, not a property of any physical source, and nothing follows for the listener: it is not consequential in the sense of Box 3.
Music therefore shows two routes to value in one signal: value inherited from consequential sources, which FSD addresses, and value from successful prediction within the music itself.
Culture and exposure.
Musical exposure is a learning history, and a culture's music shapes the distribution of signals its members meet.
Its effects are fast and specific.
Six-monthold infants detect violations of complex Balkan meters whatever their background, whereas North American adults detect violations only of meters familiar to them (Hannon and Trehub, 2005).

text.text: The Tsimane' of Bolivia, with little exposure to Western music, show no preference for consonance over dissonance although they hear the difference (McDermott et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The Tsimane' of Bolivia, with little exposure to Western music, show no preference for consonance over dissonance although they hear the difference <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(McDermott et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A prediction.
The breadth claim of Box 6 applies at the scale of a culture.
Structures inherited from voices, motion and approach have a broad functional history: every listener has heard voices and seen bodies move, whatever music they grew up with.
Their evaluative effects should therefore be comparatively stable across cultures and genres.
Structures learned within one musical system, such as particular meters or tonal syntax, have a history confined to that system, and their effects should vary with exposure.
Consonance is a boundary case: it has been related to harmonicity, which is characteristic of a single voice, yet the Tsimane' result shows that its evaluative effect depends on exposure.
The findings above are consistent with this division, though none was designed to test it.
Several accounts in aesthetics connect the perception of form with bodily or biological significance. Arnheim (1974) analysed balance, tension and direction as perceptual forces in visual art.
text.formatted: Several accounts in aesthetics connect the perception of form with bodily or biological significance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Arnheim (1974)</ref> analysed balance, tension and direction as perceptual forces in visual art.

text.text: FSD offers an explanation of why such forces should carry value: they are carried by structure that, outside art, is informative about stability, motion and support. Freedberg and Gallese (2007) proposed that viewers simulate the actions, movements and bodily states implied by a work, and Umiltà et al. (2012) found that viewing Lucio Fontana's cut canvases, but not control images with the cuts replaced by lines, suppressed the EEG mu rhythm over motor cortex, a sign of motor activation.

text.text: Both findings show that structure about action and motion is processed in still, and even abstract, images, as FSD requires; the second suggests that structure, rather than recognition of what is depicted, drives the response.
FSD differs from simulation accounts in what it takes the value to be: not the resonance of a simulated action, but evaluative weight acquired because the structure carried consequential information.

Evolutionary aesthetics attaches value to features of landscapes that once mattered for survival: places from which one can see without being seen (Appleton, 1975), or open, savanna-like settings with trees and water (Orians and Heerwagen, 1992).

text.text: FSD shares this logic but differs in two respects.

It concerns structures within objects and events rather than whole habitats, and it makes value depend on a functional history that can be extended or narrowed within a lifetime, not only on an ancestral environment.
If the principle applies to every signal that carries the structure, it should apply wherever such structures appear, and in each case it makes a prediction.

In design and architecture, structures that indicate support, load and balance should carry evaluative weight: a cantilever or an apparently unsupported mass should evoke tension even in viewers who know the building is safe, and the effect should be stronger for coarse structure seen at a distance than for detail.

Textiles carry structure that is both seen and felt: the periodicity of a weave should carry evaluative weight learned through touch as well as sight, and may share it with rhythm in music (Section 5.1).
Advertising can recruit structures such as looming or rising sound intensity to capture and colour evaluation; their effect should not require the viewer to identify what is shown.

Politics and religion enter only through the perceptual layer, for example monumental architecture or imagery: FSD may explain part of the response to a building or a staging, not the content of a belief.
Camouflage is not a case of FSD: it removes informative structure rather than recruiting its value.

Finally, design features found across cultures should be those with a broad functional history, such as stability, support and approach, whereas features confined to one tradition should have a narrow history and vary with exposure, as Section 7.1 proposes for music.
The thesis is that evaluative weight follows information about a property rather than the identity of the object.
We do not claim that the effect survives once the property can no longer be inferred; if it does, value has attached to the structure itself, a stronger result.
Property recoverability (Box 4, type (d)) is the test of that stronger claim.

The framework also leaves out, by design, value from reducing uncertainty or from prediction, and meaning fixed by convention (Section 1); and inherited weights, such as those for looming, fall outside the experiments proposed here (Section 3).

The distinctive prediction of FSD is joint: evaluative influence acquired through consequential source information should persist when its immediate practical role is reduced and transfer to new sources that preserve the informative structure, with both effects established under the same changed conditions.
The breadth of consequential functional history should predict the reach of that transfer beyond differences in perceptual sensitivity, exposure, or processing fluency.
This is a testable claim about the connection among information, valuation, and transfer, not a claim that FSD determines the evaluation of an entire artwork.
